name: Fatima Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights at Kerrow Plastics, an injection moulding plant that makes clips and door trims for car makers. I clock in at ten, take over press 7 from the day girl, and for eight hours I pull parts off, trim the flash, which is the thin bit of extra plastic, and pack them into crates. Press 7 is the oldest one, 450 tonnes, and it sulks when it's cold.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work, you can count what you made. I like the union, honestly, Denise our shop steward has saved my job once already. What wears me out is the short-time weeks. Four times this year they sent us home on 60% pay because a car maker cut its order, and I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Every year someone says robots are coming to the plastics plant, and every year it's still me pulling clips off press 7 by hand. At the union meeting I'd be the one laughing at the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI was never my worry. Short-time weeks on 60% pay, with two weeks of money in the bank, are my worry. So nothing changes for me, and that's not the same as fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and take every Saturday overtime shift going. I'd stop the Friday takeaway, that's about 30 a week, and try to get one full month saved by summer. And I'd keep paying my union dues, because that's the only insurance I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. It's the same worry on a loop, just without a robot in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first if there's another short-time month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone, then the gas if it's summer. Tomás, my partner, and I split the rent down the middle, and rent never goes late, I learned that at 22. Last time I borrowed 200 from my sister and I hated asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything at the plant changing anyway, even in this quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put a camera on press 3 last year that checks parts for flash. It saves Priya on that press maybe five minutes an hour, nothing more. If that's all AI ever is, fine by me.

say: I'd tell the union branch the **robot hype** was wrong again.
I'd point out it's still **people pulling clips** off the presses by hand.
think: My real worry is **short-time weeks** on 60% pay, not AI.
With about **two weeks saved**, one bad car order hurts every time.
do: Take every **Saturday overtime** shift on press 7.
Stop the Friday takeaway and save **about 30 a week** towards one month's cushion.
Keep paying **union dues** as the only insurance she has.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, the same worry on a loop.
S0.quote: AI was never my worry. Short-time weeks on 60% pay, with two weeks of money in the bank, are my worry.
fieldNote: Her stress comes from **car-maker orders**, not technology, and it doesn't go away when AI stalls.

Borrowing 200 from her sister still **stings**; she hates asking for help.

steps.text: Work every Saturday overtime shift going on press 7
Drop the Friday takeaway to save about 30 a week
Keep paying union dues and go to the monthly branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: if robots come in, workers get a say, and the savings don't all go to the owners. I'd share the union's posts online. I'm not going to pretend I have clever opinions about software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The writing and coding stuff doesn't touch me, I don't do any of that. What scares me is the pick-and-place arms, the robot arms that lift parts out of the mould. Slowly, to a manager, means one press a year. My press is the oldest one in the plastics plant, so it's either last in line or scrapped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Denise to get a written deal: nobody laid off when an arm goes in, they move us to packing or quality instead. I'd say yes to the quality-checking course I skipped last spring, but only if it's in paid hours. And I'd keep putting the takeaway money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like something's being decided over my head. A bit angry, and a bit small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gloria on the trim bench. She's 58 and her English isn't strong, so if they shuffle people around, she gets left out first. I'd sit with her at the meetings and make sure someone explains things to her properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any thinking work in your own day change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rota, maybe, that comes from the office. If a computer does the rota, fine, as long as it doesn't start giving me split shifts. Last thing I want is an app telling me when to sleep.

I'd share union posts online but **stay out** of software arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws, and fast. Tax the companies that use robots and pay people while they find something else. I'd go to protests, and I've never been to one in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 2028 itself doesn't scare me as much as 2031. The office people get hit first, the planners and the resin buyers. Then three years later the robot that does my job turns up, and I'll be 32 with nothing but moulding machines on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd tell the union we need a plan before 2031, not after. Tomás and I would stop talking about a bigger flat and stay where we are. And I'd have a proper talk with my mum about the back room, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like waiting for a letter you already know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years to AGI and three more for robots, what does that time actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In three years I might have one month in the bank instead of half a month. Three years sounds long until you think how little I save. That's not a plan, that's a slightly longer fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás the night the robots arrive at Kerrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say his delivery van is probably going too, so we're in it together. We'd probably laugh, because what else do you do. Then in the morning I'd ring my mum and ask about the back room for real.

say: I'd demand **laws now**: a robot tax and pay while people look for work.
I'd go to **protests** for the first time in her life.
think: The office goes first; her **press job** goes about three years later.
At 32 she'd have **only moulding** on her CV.
do: Ask the union for a **plan before 2031**, not after.
Drop the **bigger flat** and stay put with Tomás.
Talk to her mum now about the **back room** as a fallback.
feel: **Sick**, like waiting for a letter she knows is coming.

fieldNote: The three-year robot gap means little to her because her **savings barely grow**.

steps.text: Ask the union branch for a written plan before robots arrive in 2031
Join protests for a robot tax and paid time to find work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but louder, because nobody can say they didn't see it coming. Five years is plenty of time to write laws. If the government doesn't, that's a choice they made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots by 2034 means I'm 35. That's better and worse. Better because I get seven more years of wages, worse because I'd be tempted to do nothing for six of them, and I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote for whoever promises a jobs guarantee, and nag everyone on nights to vote too. I'd ask Ray, who leads maintenance, if I can shadow him on Fridays, because someone has to fix the robots for a while. And I'd open a savings account I don't touch and put 50 a month in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but not sick like the fast one. More like a bag I carry around all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2031, before the robots, the thinking AI arrives. What changes at Kerrow that year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office, mostly: planning, ordering resin, the rota. Maybe two or three people upstairs go. On the floor we'd get more short-notice shift switches, but nobody on press 7 loses a job that year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be tempted to do nothing. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having it in writing. If the union gets a date from the company, like presses get robots in 2034, then I'd move. A vague maybe never makes me move. I've ignored vague maybes my whole life.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** for laws, so doing nothing is a choice.
I'd tell the night shift to **vote** on it.

steps.text: Vote for the party promising a jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so don't waste it. Use it for proper retraining, paid and in work hours, not evening classes for people who are already worn out from nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039 is half my working life away, I'd be 40. Honestly, I'd keep doing what I do and hope the union sorts it. That's the truth, even if it doesn't sound good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working nights and keep paying dues. Push the union to make paid retraining part of the next pay deal. Anything bigger, I'd leave a few years and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. But I know calm is how I end up doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change for you and Tomás?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe kids. We've said in a few years since I was 24. With ten years, we'd still maybe do it, but I'd want the plant to still be open while the baby is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036, robots in 2039. Does that order matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, my job is all hands. I can barely work the touchscreen on the new press as it is. The office will feel 2036, and I'll feel 2039.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** that shouldn't be wasted.
I'd want retraining **paid** and in **work hours**, not tired evening classes.
think: She'd be **40** when robots arrive, half her working life away.
Honestly she'd **keep going** and hope the union sorts it.

Push the union to put **paid retraining** in the next pay deal.

steps.text: Keep working nights on press 7 and paying union dues

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. The office goes first and the floor gets three years, and three years on my savings is nothing. If a robot takes my press, the company should pay me to retrain for a year, at full wage, not 60%.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I'd let a robot train me. I wouldn't, and I know that's stubborn. I learned press 7 from a woman called Ines who'd done it 30 years, and I want the next person to learn from a person too.

name: Marco Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two injection moulding presses at Corvell Plastics, out by the ring road. We make the little clips and air vents that go inside car dashboards. I load the plastic pellets, watch the parts drop, trim the flash off with a knife and pack them in crates of 500. I've been there fourteen months and I still get told off for slow changeovers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm when a press runs clean, and I like Dev, the setter who eats lunch with me and shows me tricks. What wears me out is the heat by the hoppers and the twelve-hour weekend shifts. My partner Priya works in a care home, so between her rota and mine we sometimes only see each other on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the plant didn't need another thing to worry about. In the canteen we'd joke that the robot uprising got cancelled. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should have gone into nurses and buses instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't fix anything for me. My pay is still the lowest grade, the rent on our flat still goes up every spring, and Corvell still only has one big customer. If that car maker sneezes, we're the ones on short weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the presses and try to get signed off on changeovers so I move up a pay band. I'd keep using the chatbot now and then, like when I asked it to explain mould temperatures. And I'd go to the union meeting in the spring, because the pay talks are what actually matter to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a bit of relief mixed with the same old tightness in my chest at the end of the month. Nothing new to fear, but nothing new to hope for either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Corvell has one big customer. Has that ever bitten you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter the car maker cut its orders and we went to four-day weeks for six weeks. I lost about a fifth of my pay and we put the heating bill on the credit card. Priya picked up extra shifts and I felt useless about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight again, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car insurance on my old Fiesta is the big one, but I need the car to get to nights. So it'd be takeaways, my phone contract and the gym first. The rent never waits, so everything else bends around the rent.

say: I'd tell people the **robot uprising** got cancelled and the plant can breathe.
I'd post that the money should go to **nurses and buses**, not hype.
think: The plateau changes nothing about my **lowest-grade pay** or rising rent.
Corvell depends on **one car maker**, so short weeks are the real threat.
do: Get signed off on **changeovers** this year to move up a pay band.
Go to the **union meeting** in spring because pay talks matter most.
Keep using the chatbot **now and then** to learn press settings.
feel: He feels **relief** that no new threat is coming.
The usual **end-of-month tightness** in his chest stays exactly the same.
S0.quote: The rent never waits, so everything else bends around the rent.
fieldNote: His worry in a calm world comes from **one big customer**, not from AI.
Last winter's **four-day weeks** cost him a fifth of his pay and still sting.
He sees the **union** as his main lever, more than any technology.
Feels guilty that **Priya** covered the gap with extra shifts.

steps.text: Get signed off on mould changeovers to reach the next pay band
Attend the spring union meeting on the new pay deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office that's going to feel it first, not us on the floor. The planners and the people who answer the car maker's emails, that's where the software goes. At the union meeting I'd push for a rule that nobody gets cut without retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it hits me sideways. If the office gets cheaper, Corvell might spend the savings on a robot arm that picks parts off the press, and that's half my job. Dev says two plants up north already have them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor, Gemma, to put me on the robot arm training if it comes, before someone else grabs it. I'd use the chatbot more to learn the basics of how those arms are set up. I'd also stop the gym membership and put that thirty a month into savings, because one month of cushion is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not frozen. It feels like there's a queue forming and I'd better be near the front of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Ray on the packing bench, he's 58 and can barely work his phone. If they bring in a robot that boxes the parts, he's done, and nobody's going to retrain a man two years from his pension. That's exactly the kind of person the union should fight for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office gets hit first. Does that make you feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year or two, maybe. But it's not safe, it's just later. If they need fewer people planning and checking, they'll want fewer people on the floor too once the arms are cheap. On the factory floor we're not safe from AI, we're just later in the queue.

transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2028 the planners and the quality office are gone, and by 2031 the presses run themselves. I'd be 32 with no trade and no savings. Priya's job caring for old people might last longer than mine, which is a strange thing to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd start the evening maintenance course at the college, the one Dev did, because fixing robots lasts longer than running presses. I'd sell the Fiesta and get a bike if the bus covers nights. And I'd be at every union meeting, pushing for redundancy pay of at least a month per year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Two years is nothing when you're starting with one month of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 2031 look like in your street?

transcript.speaker: persona

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Halden Precision, a shop of about forty people that turns brass valve parts and pump shafts. I run two CNC lathes, which are lathes a computer steers, so mostly I load bar stock, start the program, measure parts with a micrometer and swap worn tool tips. I'm still slow at setting the tools, so Stan, the senior machinist, checks my first part every morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a part comes off shiny and inside tolerance, which means within the allowed size, about the width of a hair. I spend my breaks asking an AI chatbot to explain the G-code, the language the lathe reads, line by line. What wears me out is the pay, honestly. I share a flat with two housemates and I still have about three weeks of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. I'd post something like: all that noise and we still have kids who can't afford rent. At work I'd say at least Stan can stop telling me the robots are coming for my lathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm stuck on the bottom rate unless I push myself. The tools I use every day would still help me learn faster than the others. But there's only Halden and one other machine shop in town, so if I don't move up here, I don't move up anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking the chatbot to walk me through programs until I can write simple ones myself. I'd ask Stan to let me do my own tool setting by spring. And I'd join the union at Halden, because there's only eleven of us in it and the pay review is in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. I was half excited for something big to happen, and now it's just rent and three weeks of savings again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, half excited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I grew up watching my mum do the same packing job for twenty years. Part of me wanted the world to shake up so I wouldn't end up the same. When nothing happens, the old life just carries on, and the old life doesn't pay much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill frightens you most right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat's heating, because the landlord's boiler is ancient and the bill jumped last winter. My housemate Leo and I split it, and I covered his half one month when he was short. I can't do that twice.

Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the bottling line at Brightwater Drinks, the soft drinks plant by the canal. My job is the filler and the capper: I feed in the cap hoppers, clear jams, swap the labels when we change flavour and pull bottles for the quality check. I've been there just over a year and I'm still the one they send to clear the sticky jams.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's simple, you know where you are. Same line, same lads, same break at ten. What wears me out is the noise and the rotating shifts, mornings one week and nights the next. My girlfriend Jess works mornings at a bakery counter, so we pass each other in the hallway half the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so. Everyone was getting worked up about computers taking over and it came to nothing. I don't go online much, but down the pub I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, I was already worried before any of this. Brightwater lost a supermarket contract in the summer and we went off weekend overtime, and overtime is what pays my rent. There's the drinks plant, a warehouse and not much else round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my shifts. I'd ask the shift lead, Phil, if any overtime comes back, and I'd take every hour. I'm not one for courses or apps, I'd rather just be reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, if I'm honest. AI not happening doesn't put money back in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much was the overtime worth to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred a month, on a good month. Without it, Jess and I go short in the last week, beans on toast and no going out. Last month I borrowed fifty off my brother to cover the electric.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the plant cut hours again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go round the warehouse and ask for agency shifts. I don't like agency work, you never know if you're on until the night before. But fifty quid from my brother isn't something I want to make a habit of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office types who should worry, not us. Computers writing emails don't clear a jam on a capper. I'd say that at work and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not so sure. If the office gets cheaper, Brightwater has more money for a new line, and the new lines barely need anyone. At a plant open day I saw two people running a bottling line that we run with six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and hope I'm one of the two. I'd probably ask Phil what the new line would need, but I wouldn't do some course on a computer. I'd stop the takeaway on Fridays and try to put a bit by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach. I'm not good with new things, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you one of the two people who stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Turning up, not being sick, knowing the line. That's what's always counted before. Maybe that's not enough anymore, but it's what I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Phil. What if he says you need training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, I suppose, if they paid and it was in work time. I wouldn't pay for it myself, I haven't got the money and I'd be no good at it at night after a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody in charge had better sort it out, because people like me can't. I'd probably shout about it down the pub. I'm not the sort to march, but I'd vote for whoever promised to protect jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished at Brightwater by 2031. The office goes in 2028, and three years later the robots can clear jams better than me. I've got no trade, no savings and no idea what else I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd keep working while there was work and take every bit of overtime. I'd probably ask my brother about labouring on the building sites, though if robots can do hands-on work, that goes too. Jess and I would have to give up the flat and move in with her mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like the floor's going and there's nothing to grab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jess that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm sorry, and that I don't know what to do. My girlfriend Jess believes in me more than I do, and I'd hate to let her down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If someone offered you free retraining, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to say yes. But retraining for what, if the robots come three years later for whatever I learn? I'd probably just keep turning up until they told me not to.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. I'd tell the lads to keep their heads and see what the company offers. Same as always, I'd say it to people's faces, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deep down, it's the same as the fast one, just later. I'd be 32 when the robots get good, and I still don't fancy my chances learning computers. But five years might be enough to save a bit and see where the jobs are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Brightwater if they'd train me on the new line before it comes. I'd try to save fifty a month, even if it means no holiday. And I'd keep an eye on the jobs at the water treatment works, because my uncle reckons those are steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. A bit less panicky than the fast one, but heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's at the water treatment works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Dieter checks pumps and valves there, mostly walking round with a clipboard and a torch. He says they'd never trust a robot with drinking water. I don't know if he's right, but he's been there thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a job there for less money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For steady, yes. I'd rather earn a bit less and know I'm on next month. That's all I want really, to know I'm on next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer for now, but I know that's partly me burying my head.

transcript.text: What would you want to be different from your dad's story?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to have something lined up before the gate closes. My dad sat in the kitchen for a year after the steelworks shut. I don't want Jess watching me do the same.

transcript.speaker: persona

name: Priya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two injection moulding machines at Brightpak, a plant on the edge of town that makes plastic food tubs and lids. Moulding means melting plastic pellets and squirting them into a steel mould, then the part pops out. I start at six, check the hopper's full, watch the first parts for flash, which is the thin extra plastic around the edge, and box what comes off the conveyor. I've been there just over a year, so I still call the setter, Kwame, when a mould sticks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you live with, and how are things at home money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, the part that wears me out is the noise and standing on concrete for eight hours. The part I like is when a whole run comes out clean and I've caught a problem before it turned into two thousand bad lids. I'm in the union, and I go to the meetings in the canteen even though half of it is people complaining about the vending machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the canteen: told you so. Every year the bosses promise some new system will change everything, and we still end up scraping lids off the floor by hand. Online I'd probably share a meme about it and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Brightpak lost a big supermarket contract last spring, and we went down to four-day weeks for two months. If AI is a flop, the lost supermarket contract and the four-day weeks are still sitting there. Nothing changing isn't the same as everything being fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep learning the machines properly, so I'm not the weakest one if they cut a shift. I'd keep putting about a hundred a month into savings, because we've got roughly three months put by. And I'd push at the union meeting to get short-time pay written down properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat, a bit tired. It's the same low hum of worry I already carry every time the order board looks thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dev, my partner, that it's one less thing on the pile but the pile's still there. He works nights at a parcel depot, so between us we're always one bad month from dipping into savings. We'd still skip the holiday and keep the money where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kwame, the setter, actually. He's the only one who really knows the old moulds, and if he left, the line would fall apart. Management keeps saying they'll train someone else, and they never do.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if your hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership goes first, then eating out on Fridays. Dev and I would keep the rent and the car paid before anything. The car matters because the bus doesn't reach the plant before six.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I run two injection moulding machines at a plant on Mill Road that makes plastic caps for drinks bottles. Most weeks I'm on nights, which is why the pay's decent, and I spend the shift watching the counters, checking caps for flash and short shots, and topping up the colour pellets. I've been there just over a year, so I'm still slow on mould changes and I lean on the setter a lot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's steady and I know what's coming every night. I'm in the union and the rep, a woman called Gloria, actually picks up the phone when you ring. What wears me out is the noise and the heat off the barrels, and the robot arm on machine six that jams and makes me look bad on the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I told you so. Every few months someone in the canteen says the machines will run themselves, and here we are, still running them. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my life stays the way I like it, and the only thing that changes is the planning office gets some software. I've got about nine months of pay saved from the years I lived with my gran, and the shift premium keeps it growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my nights and keep putting a third of my pay into savings. I'd finally ask the setter to train me properly on mould changes, because that's the bit holding me back. I wouldn't touch any of the AI stuff, there'd be no reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Calm. It's the boring version and boring suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that still bothers you about the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The heat and the nights, if I'm honest. My partner works days at the hospital and some weeks we only see each other on Sunday. That's not an AI thing, that's just the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for proper training on mould changes. What's stopped you so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, a bit. I don't like looking slow in front of the older lads. In the boring version I'd have no excuse left, so I'd swallow it and ask.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a kitchen furniture factory, on the cabinet door line. I run a CNC router, which is a computer-controlled cutter that shapes the doors from big boards, and then an edge-bander that glues the trim on the edges. I load the boards, pick the right program off the screen, and check the doors for chips. Nine months in, and I still mix up the programs for the two shaker styles now and then.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona

opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. My girlfriend Leila works nights at a care home, so we pass each other in the hallway, and after rent and the car loan there's maybe a few hundred left at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. At work we'd laugh about it on break, because the managers kept sending emails about smart factories and nothing happened. Online I'd probably post something about how the money should have gone into our wages instead of software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't really fix anything for me. The plant cut the night shift last spring because the car maker ordered less, and that has nothing to do with AI. I'm still on low pay with less than a month saved, so a quiet AI future just means the same tight life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep going to the union meetings, because that's where the real fight is, over pay and hours. I'd try to pick up the Saturday overtime when it's offered, which is maybe two Saturdays a month. I'm not going to learn computer stuff for a future that didn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, then back to normal worry. It's like the storm missed us, but the roof was already leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's maybe a few hundred left each month. What happens when a big bill lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter the car needed a new clutch and it cost almost a whole month's rent. We put it on a card and we're still paying it off. A car repair is enough to put Leila (his girlfriend) and me behind for half a year, and AI has nothing to do with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI doesn't change much, what does keep you up at night about the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Orders. If the car maker moves the contract to a cheaper plant abroad, we're done, robots or no robots. Rosa keeps saying the new manager is looking at costs, and when they look at costs they look at us.

opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.text: I like that I can hear when something's wrong before the screen tells me. There's a rattle the capper makes before it jams, and I love catching it. What wears me out is the twelve hours on concrete and the pay, which is lower than the brewery in the city, but the brewery's an hour away and I don't drive. I rent a room in a shared house on Mill Street, and I've got about two weeks' rent saved if anything goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.text: Honestly, it's a bit of a relief, but my life's still tight. I'm still on low pay, still one bad month from asking my mum for money. The plant's fine for now, but nothing about AI going quiet fixes the rent.

transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, but tired. Nothing's on fire, but nothing's getting better either.

opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

I share a flat with my friend Chiara, and I've got maybe two weeks' rent saved after paying off my scooter.

name: Gareth Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a press line at Corbett Pressings. We stamp metal brackets and hinges for car seats and doors. It's four days on, four off, twelve hours, six till six. I start by checking the die is seated right, run the first parts and put them on the gauge before the line goes. After that it's feeding coil, watching for splits, clearing jams and keeping the bins moving so the forklift drivers aren't waiting on me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm of a 400-tonne press when it's running sweet, honestly. I like Dave Kowalski, my shift lead, who's been there thirty years and can hear a die cracking before it shows. What wears me out is the night block in winter and the overtime going up and down with the car orders. Last spring we had three weeks of short time after Corbett lost a contract, and we had to dip into our savings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a little about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Hannah is a dental nurse. We rent a two-bed flat on Mill Road, ten minutes from the plant. We've got about three months of bills put away and we're building a house deposit, slowly. My mum and dad live five minutes away and we're there every Sunday for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That sounds a lot like now, to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly. At break the lads talk about robots taking over every few months, and nothing ever happens at our place. Online I wouldn't bother, I only post about football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my worry, the order book is. If Corbett loses another car contract, we go back on short time whether there's AI or not. The office might use it for scheduling, which is fine by me if the rota stops changing at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up and take the overtime when it's going. Hannah and I would keep putting 200 a month in the house fund and leave the three months of bills untouched. I've been meaning to ask about the setter course, the people who change the dies, so I'd probably finally do it, because setters get kept on when it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled, but not relaxed. Short time last spring still sits with me. A normal year for us still has a wobble in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said setters get kept on when it's quiet. Who goes first if the orders drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agency staff first, then the newer operators. I'm in the middle, five years in, so not first but not safe either. Marek, the setter I eat lunch with, says setters never get laid off because nobody else can change a die in under an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If short time came again, what gets cut at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday goes first, we'd planned a week by the sea in June. Then takeaways and my gym membership. The house fund would stop, which is the bit that really stings, because every month we stop saving is another month paying someone else's mortgage.

transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.text: At work I'd say what my dad used to say, that machines come and you change with them. I'd probably say it louder than I believe it. Online I might share something about apprenticeships, because that's the bit everyone forgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the office gets it first, the planners and the buyers, and we'd see fewer of them. On the floor, Corbett would put a robot arm on the unload end of my press, because that's the easy bit, picking a bracket off a belt. Then I'm minding two presses instead of one, and they need half the operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the setter course for definite, and I'd ask to be on whatever robot cell they put in first, because whoever learns it first keeps a job. transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap is simple. I'd tell everyone you change with the machines, but I've had one press job since college and never changed with anything. I believe it's right for the country, I'm just not sure I'm the one who'll do it well.

transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be counting. AGI in 2028 means the planners and buyers at Corbett are gone straight away. Robots on the floor by 2031 means I'd be 32 with no job and a skill nobody needs. Three extra years is not long when you've only ever stood at a press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into a proper trade straight away, maybe maintenance electrician, because somebody has to fix the robots for a while. I'd ask Corbett to sponsor the apprenticeship and do nights at college if they won't. We'd stop the house hunt and keep the deposit as a cushion. I'd also talk to my dad, because he went through the steelworks closing.

name: Nora Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. opening.text: I run filler line three at Brookfield Drinks, a soft-drinks bottling plant on the edge of town. opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a clean changeover, going from lemon to cola in under forty minutes when everyone's in sync. What wears me out is the labeller, which jams if the glue is a degree too cold, and the ringing in my ears at night. And standing on concrete for eight hours, my feet feel thirty years older than me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My fiancé Tom is a joiner, he fits kitchens and staircases. We rent a terrace on Station Street, and the wedding's next August at my church, where I sing in the choir. We've got about four months of bills saved, but the wedding is eating into it. I'm also doing an online course at night on PLCs, the little computers that run the line, with an AI tutor on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a bit of a letdown, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it'd be fine. I'd keep using the AI tools for what they're good at, which is explaining fault codes and helping me study, and I'd keep moving toward a technician job. Brookfield is busy, summer orders keep going up, and the plant isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the PLC course by March and apply for the line technician post when Sandra Mensah, my shift manager, opens it in spring. transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight but planned. The church hall is booked, my aunt is doing the cake, and Tom is building our wedding arch himself from oak offcuts. My dad always said debt for a day is debt for years, so my fiancé Tom and I will never borrow for the wedding.

opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona

Never have.

transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief, and I'd feel a bit smug. My job is in my hands and my ears, not on a screen, so some software in the office doesn't touch me. The real fight at Kessler stays what it's always been: pay, shifts and safety.

transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep my shifts, keep putting about a fifth of my pay aside each month, and keep going to the union meetings. Inés and I were already thinking about a deposit on a flat near the hospital in a couple of years, and I'd stick to that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell any apprentice to join the union on day one and learn to listen to the machine. A good operator who knows his rights will always find work in this town. There are four plants within twenty minutes of my flat.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run four injection moulding machines at Corvel Medical, out on the industrial estate by the river. I've been there six years.

opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona

What wears me out is nights every third week and the gown in summer. My partner Sam drives the number 14 bus, so our shifts barely line up. I use one of those AI chat apps now and then, mostly to help write letters to our landlord.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes. My work is hands and eyes in a clean room, and some scheduling software in the office isn't going to load a mould. I'd still have a decent job in a town with plenty of plants.

transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, if anything.

transcript.speaker: persona

opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Jade. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name stays off it. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.text: I run injection moulding machines at a plant that makes medical plastics, mostly syringe barrels and parts for asthma inhalers. opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. Somewhere a nurse is using a syringe I checked, and I take that seriously. The hard part is the twelve-hour shifts on the four-on, four-off rota, and the heat coming off the machines even with the air system running. Agnieszka, the older operator I train with, says you stop noticing the hum after five years, and I'm nearly there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Tomás, he's an electrician, and we're getting married next June at my parish church. We've saved a good house deposit between us, more than six months of both our wages, because we both grew up in families where you didn't buy what you couldn't pay for. I use AI now and then, mostly to help word things, like the wedding invitations, but not much more than that.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona

name: Rafael Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Rafael. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.text: I run two five-axis CNC machines, computer-controlled milling machines, at a precision shop that makes hydraulic valve bodies for tractors and diggers. I load the aluminium blanks, set the tool offsets, start the program, and then measure the finished parts with micrometers and the measuring machine in the quality room. opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.text: I like the precision, getting a bore right to a hundredth of a millimetre. I ask an AI assistant to explain the G-code, the instructions the machine reads, or to translate the German manual for the new spindle. My foreman Hugo calls me the professor, half as a joke.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside the shop?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got a small flat with a mortgage I'm paying down fast, and about ten months of pay saved. On weekends I rent a garage unit with an old manual mill and a 3D printer, and I make custom motorbike parts that I sell online. My girlfriend Ana is a primary school teacher, and Sunday is Mass with my parents and lunch at theirs, no exceptions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.text: I like being the one people come to. When press four starts throwing out warped lids and nobody knows why, I can usually hear it before I see it. What wears me out is the pay. transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.text: Who decides when short-time happens?

transcript.speaker: persona

opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Adam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead setter on the CNC lathes at Kessel Components. We turn brake discs and hub parts for two car makers. A CNC lathe is a machine that cuts metal following a program, and my job is setting it up, loading the right tools, running the first piece and measuring it before the run goes. I've got four lads on my shift and six machines, and I'm usually the one with a micrometer in my hand at the end of the line.

opening.text: Best part is when a new job runs perfect on the first piece. You feel like a craftsman for a second. Hardest part is the money, honestly. transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona

I take a photo of the screen and ask an AI app what it means and what to check first. I do that every day now, and it's saved me hours. The engineers upstairs think I'm cheating; I think they're slow.

She lives with her partner Tom, a **warehouse worker**, and they're saving slowly for a wedding.
**Pragmatic** and centrist, she uses AI now and then and learns new tools once proven.
Her main fear is **both incomes** failing together, especially in the fast scenarios.
With more warning she plans a **maintenance certificate** and keeps care work as plan B.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would take both her job and Tom's with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Free weekend courses** so people can earn while learning.
Honest information about **which jobs** will last.

name: Erik Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for taking part, Erik. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and your answers are confidential. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead operator on the press line at Tallis Panels. We make chipboard, the stuff inside cheap furniture and kitchen worktops. Wood chips and glue go in one end, and a sixty-metre press squeezes them into boards at about two hundred degrees. I watch the screens, walk the line, check board thickness and sort out the forming station when the chips clump.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you enjoy?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Finding patterns. I started logging every stoppage in a spreadsheet two years ago, and I use an AI chat every day to help me spot what they have in common. Turns out half our jams happen when the chips come from one supplier on wet days. I showed the manager and she changed the order schedule. That felt good, even if the pay didn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Bit of an anticlimax, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and people got carried away. At work I'd say keep using it for the boring stuff, like I do with the stoppage log. Online I'd stay out of it; the arguments are tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the problem stays the same: I'm good at this and I'm paid like I'm not. I've got about two weeks of money saved, Maya (my girlfriend) rents a chair at a hair salon and her money goes up and down, and Tallis is the only board plant for eighty kilometres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep improving the line and keep the stoppage log, because that's how I get noticed. I'd ask for a pay review in January with my numbers on paper. And I'd grow the side thing I do, fixing 3D printers for people and selling spare parts online, which makes about a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit frustrated. Like I'm running fast on a short lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on paper for the pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stoppage hours down from forty a month to twenty-six since I started the log. I'd ask the AI to help me turn that into money saved, because managers listen to money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the review says no, then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the printer repairs get more of my evenings. I wouldn't leave Tallis yet, there's nothing else around. But I'd be building a way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 an AI can read the stoppage data better than me, so my clever bit is gone. I've got three years on the hands-on part, until the robots can clear a clumped forming station. I'm adaptable, but I've got two weeks of savings, and you can't adapt on nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year becoming the person who installs and looks after the robots when they arrive. transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Maya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say her job might actually outlast mine, because nobody wants a robot cutting their hair yet. Then I'd say we need to save like it's winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is close to perfect for me. I'd have time to get a proper automation qualification and save a bit. By 2031 the thinking AI arrives, and I'd want to already be the person who knows how to run AI on a factory floor. Then I'd have three more years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an automation technician course next year, part-time, and ask Tallis to help pay. I'd put the printer money into a savings account, not the bike fund. And I'd look at a better-paid plant within a couple of hours, once I had the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more fired up than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said save the printer money. How much a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About twelve hundred, if I'm strict. Twelve hundred saved would be three months of rent, the biggest cushion I've ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tallis could close before the robots even come, if the owners decide it's cheaper to build a new robot plant somewhere else. That's the real fear. Then all my clever plans need a new address.
