name: Fatima Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good evening, Fatima, and thank you for seeing me before your shift. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working night?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the oven line at Golden Crust, the big bakery on the ring road. We do sliced bread and rolls for the supermarkets, about forty thousand loaves a night. I start at ten, check the proofer, that's the warm room where the dough rises, then I set the oven zones and watch the colour of the crust all night. If the bake's wrong, two hours of bread goes in the skip, so I don't take my eyes off it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. Families eat what I bake at breakfast. My grandmother baked bread by hand in her village, and I tell her I bake forty thousand a night and she laughs. What's hard is the nights, and the pay. I'm the senior on the line and I'm still on less than the day supervisors, and there's no other bakery like this for fifty kilometres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I never trusted all that talk anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my father says: hard work doesn't go out of fashion. At work I'd tell the young ones to stop worrying about computers and learn the ovens properly. I don't post things online. I'd say it after church, maybe, if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things stay hard but honest. I have less than a month of money saved, and Piotr (my fiancé), who's an electrician's apprentice, and I are saving for the wedding in June. The night premium is what makes the money work, and Golden Crust keeps talking about cutting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working nights and do every extra shift I'm offered. I'd ask my uncle if Piotr and I could rent his upstairs flat cheaper after the wedding. And I'd keep the wedding small, sixty people at the parish hall, not a hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Tired, but steady. I trust God and my own hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they talk about cutting the night premium. What happens if they do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I lose about a hundred and fifty a month. We'd still marry in June, I'm not moving that. But we'd live at my uncle's and the honeymoon would be a weekend at the lake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at AI tools for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've never used them and I don't need to. My mother runs the house on a notebook and it works fine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Marco. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.text: I'm lead operator on the corrugator at Ashby Packaging. The corrugator is the long machine that glues paper into cardboard sheets, the brown board that boxes are made from. My dad worked thirty years at the paper mill up the road, so I grew up with the smell of it.

opening.text: What's good about it and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is the crew. We're like a football team, and when a big order goes through clean, we all know it. Hard is the pay. I'm the best on the corrugator and I'm paid less than the Ashby plant in the city. And with the paper mill closed, there's only us left in town.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's mostly noise. That's what my dad would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my worries are the same as now. Rosa (my girlfriend) is a teaching assistant and neither of us earns much. We've got about three weeks saved and the rent went up again. Ashby's had two quiet months this year, and when it's quiet, the overtime goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the corrugator and keep my crew tight, because a good crew keeps a plant open. I'd ask Ashby about the electrical apprenticeship they talk about every year but never start. And I'd use the AI app now and then, like when I checked our tenancy agreement last month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Not worried, just stuck where I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the plant had two quiet months. What did that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred in lost overtime. We skipped Rosa's sister's wedding abroad because of it. She still mentions it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think the apprenticeship never starts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because head office sees it as a cost. My dad did his apprenticeship at sixteen and the mill paid for all of it. Companies used to take the long view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the filling line to keep running, yet my low wage leaves little room if a shift is cancelled. With less than a month saved and few other factories nearby, even the ordinary bills make me careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first pack check after a changeover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I pull a sealed pouch and test the seam, then check the weight and label. If the seam opens, I stop the line before a whole batch is spoiled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

name: Colin Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm senior setter on the big injection moulding presses at Halden Plastics, on the ring road estate. We make door panels and dashboard trims for two car makers. My shift starts at six, I walk the four presses, check the moulds are running clean, sort the scrap bins, and fix whatever the night shift left me. The best part is a tool change done in under forty minutes; the worst is standing over a 900-tonne press in August.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part of the job only you can do, the bit people come to you for?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Reading a bad part. A door panel comes out with a sink mark or a short shot, and I can usually tell you if it's the barrel heat, the hold pressure or a blocked vent before anyone opens a screen. I'm also the union rep for our shift, so people come to me when the rota goes wrong. I've been there since I was nineteen, and I know those presses like my own kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's what I already think is happening. Everyone talks about AI, but on our floor the thing that changed things was a robot arm on Press 4, and that had nothing to do with chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. In the break room I'd tell the lads that the hype was the bosses' excuse to scare us into taking a flat pay deal. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be watching that robot arm on Press 4. Plateau or not, the company put it in last spring to take parts out of the mould, and it cost us one job on each shift. AI stalling doesn't stop them buying more arms like that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, keep the presses running and keep my head down. I'd push at the next union meeting for a written deal that any new robot comes with retraining, not redundancy. And I'd keep putting £150 a month away, because we're renting and Ines (my partner) wants a place of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, but not relaxed. The rent went up again in September, and the car makers keep cutting their orders. So even with AI going nowhere, I'm not sleeping on a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot arm cost one job on each shift. Who was that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, who'd been on the press for twelve years. He got moved to packing on less money, and he never says a word about it, but you can see it. That's the thing I'm watching for, more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your manager offered you a course on the new arm's controls, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'm good at what I do, and I don't want to spend my evenings learning to babysit the thing that pushed Marek out. Ines says I'm stubborn, and she's right.

name: Emeka Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a cell of computer-controlled milling machines making metal housings for medical pumps. My two-year technical diploma taught me how to set a tool path; on the floor I learned to hear when a cutter is wearing out. I use AI every day to draft setup notes and look up fault codes, then verify the answer against the machine manual and the finished part. I live alone, earn a higher operator rate, have more than six months of expenses saved, and know several plants nearby that need machine people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a modest AI tool can save us time finding a fault code, but it cannot measure a finished housing. I already use it for notes and check the part with a gauge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cell has orders and the work stays mostly physical, so I expect my pay to hold. Savings and nearby plants give me room to test useful tools without making every software update a career decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the milling machines and comparing AI-drafted notes with the manual. In the first year I would ask the junior operator to measure the first housing with me before either of us signs a batch off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a little curious. A machine can make a precise part only after somebody notices the cutter has worn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a worn cutter look like in the part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The edge gets a fine burr that catches my glove, and the gauge may still pass the main width. We stop before the whole tray is made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust the AI fault answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only as a pointer into the manual. A confident answer cannot take responsibility for a medical pump housing that fails inspection.

opening.text: I am forty-three and a junior operator on a fabric printing press at a textile factory. I finished secondary school and am still learning how much ink the rollers need; the lead checks my first length after a colour change. I like seeing a pattern come out clean, though washing a clogged roller is slow. I use an AI assistant every day to sort print-fault notes, but I compare them with the cloth. My husband and I have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is ordinary for this work, we have about three months of expenses saved, and some similar factories are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew an AI fault note is handy, but the cloth still has to match the sample. The fabric edge still shows every ink smear after the AI writes its clean report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The printing shifts and typical pay should carry on. Three months saved and some nearby factories give us room, and I am glad I can keep learning from the lead without a sudden change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the fabric rollers and checking the first printed length with the lead. I would add a new amount from each full paid month to our mortgage buffer after ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work continuing. A useful tool is welcome, but I still trust the cloth in my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you look for in the first length?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hold the cloth against the colour sample and check whether the border is sharp. If ink bleeds into the pale strip, I stop and clean the roller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the mortgage buffer new money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three months already saved stay put. I would add a fresh transfer from this month’s wages after food and school costs.

I finished secondary school and am still junior; the lead checks my first block after a mould change because I sometimes leave one edge soft. I feed the mix, clear the press and watch the curing racks. The union rate is high for this job, we have nine months of expenses saved and there are plenty of similar plants nearby. transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our higher union wage and regular block orders should carry on. Nine months saved and many nearby plants give us room if one factory has trouble, so I am comfortable with this modest picture.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A block can crumble when the mix is too dry or the mould is not packed evenly. I set the first one aside and ask the lead to check the next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you add to nine months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona

name: Jade Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day on your factory lines like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run three bagging lines at a frozen vegetable plant. The peas come through a hopper, the machines weigh and seal them, and I change the film rolls and clear jams. The packing hall is four degrees, so I keep a second fleece in my locker even in summer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day comes home with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The shift pattern, more than the cold. Harvest brings long days, then winter brings shorter weeks, and our mortgage does not follow the pea crop. My partner Dan drives parcels, and we have two children at school; I sometimes use an AI app for a shopping list or homework, but not on the lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the packing crew the big AI promises have fizzled and our baggers still need hands at the film rolls. The winter shift board worries me more than an AI headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can do the job, but last winter a quarter of my wages went missing for three months when the shifts shortened. We have less than a month put aside and very few similar plants nearby. A quiet AI future does not make that mortgage payment easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.text: I would stay on the three lines and put a fixed slice of every harvest overtime payment into a separate winter account. Dan and I would use our Sunday bill list before we agree to any extra spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the winter pay cut even with AI doing very little. The line work itself feels familiar, which helps me get through a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much did the shorter winter weeks change your bills last time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We used Dan’s Christmas delivery overtime and then the credit card. I hated opening the card statement after the holidays. A small harvest transfer would give us something to use before borrowing again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the plant would you most want to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the handover between shifts. Our quality checker calls out a weight problem before a whole pallet is wrong, and I trust that more than a bright screen. The work is cold, but the people know their line.

opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary shift like on your factory line?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the filler and capper at a milk bottling plant. A capper makes a small wrong sound before it cross-threads a lid, and I stop the line before milk goes across the floor. I have a vocational certificate, but hearing that sound took years of shifts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do the shifts mean for life at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tom drives buses, and we trade school pickup for our two children around his rota and my early starts. I use an AI app occasionally to explain a fault code, then check the actual manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once named a sensor our capper does not have. I wasted ten minutes looking for it before opening the manual. The capper manual wins every argument with my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you raise about washdown?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The line is called finished when the last bottle leaves, yet we still clean the filler for nearly an hour. I would ask the union representative to bring the paid-time record to the next plant meeting. That is a wage issue we already have.

name: Erik Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on your usual factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two computer-controlled milling machines. I load aluminium blocks, set the cutting tools and measure parts for aircraft fittings and hospital equipment. A part that is a fraction out goes into scrap; I like tracing whether heat, a blunt tool or my own program caused it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the rest of your week like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have a vocational certificate and nearly three months of expenses saved. My wife Mira works nights at a hospital, so I usually take our two children to school before an afternoon shift; we also pay a mortgage. I use an AI assistant daily to explain manuals and suggest program checks, but I verify every dimension myself. Our factory has no union yet, and I have been talking with coworkers about forming one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my machinist friends that AI still helps with a manual but has not learned to measure a warm part. I would post that workers should get a fair share of any scrap savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am mostly secure if the machines still need a setter. We have almost three months saved and some other shops nearby, though Mira’s night rota means my shift choices are limited. I would be a little disappointed that the tools stopped improving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the two milling machines and document which AI suggestions actually prevented scrap, checking every result with a gauge. I would also invite coworkers to a first meeting about union recognition, since our factory still has no collective voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my wage in this picture. I would miss the technical puzzle that a stronger tool might have brought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the scrap record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The part number, the tool age and the measurement before and after I changed the program. My manager can read a page of numbers faster than an argument about a chatbot. I want evidence before asking for a paid tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why organise a union if AI barely changes?

Her **bus-driver partner**, two school-age children, mortgage, year-plus reserve and rented flat give her room to bargain and choose.
She has **never used AI**, distrusts untested screens and brings paid-time and safety records to her union committee.
Fast robots threaten **press hours**, while longer warning permits conditional inspection training and extra mortgage payments from wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives little time to protect press wages before capable robots reach the line around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **wage-backed transfer**, posted adequate jobs and union involvement before equipment decisions would help.

name: Aaron Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I set three CNC lathes making hydraulic fittings for tractors and diggers. CNC means the machine follows a programmed cut; I load bar stock, set tools and measure the first fitting. I hold a vocational certificate and earn above the usual operator rate after eleven years, though a broken tool still spoils my afternoon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and what tools do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Maya works as a nurse, and our school-age children Sofia and Daniel live with us under the same mortgage. We have about ten months saved, partly because I went through a factory closure before; other machine shops are nearby. I use an AI chat tool now and then to explain drawing notes, after checking the printed dimensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the lads at the lathes that a useful drawing note beats a grand AI forecast. The hydraulic fitting still has to pass a micrometer check before it leaves my station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machines and my higher wage can carry on, and Maya’s nursing pay gives us another income. We have ten months saved because I remember how the bakery-equipment plant closed, not because I expect trouble every Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting my three lathes and checking the first part of each batch. I would keep using a chat tool now and then for drawing notes, as I already do, and put a fresh amount from full paid months into our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm in this picture. There is plenty of similar machine work nearby if this firm loses one contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the old plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer left, the orders thinned, and then the doors closed. That is why I like seeing ten months of bills in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a new tool now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test a new drawing feature only if it solved a real lathe problem. At the moment I use the same chat tool as before, so there is no new training planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the union should get a look at new machine plans before a camera appears on our floor. If the firm gains output, the people who set the tools deserve paid training and a share of the gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering and programming could move to software before robots spread into hands-on loading. My tool-setting hours might shrink, even though there are other plants nearby and Maya’s nurse wage and our reserve give us time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union rep for the planned staffing numbers and watch two colleagues try the new system. If the college offers a funded CAM programming place after my shift, and Maya can cover the children those evenings, I would enrol and learn to write toolpaths; I would also practise a new AI drawing checker on my own parts only after the firm provides paid training and a safe test copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own hours, but I can try a course without putting the mortgage on a card. I want to see a clean cut, not a sales slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether a real seat is open, who pays the fee, and when the two evening classes finish. Maya’s hospital rota must cover Sofia and Daniel before I accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the drawing checker change a setting automatically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would compare its suggested dimensions with the print and measure a scrap part before any paid batch. A qualified setter should be beside me for the first trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch that thinking AGI could program lathes by 2028, while capable hands-on robots arrive around 2031. A quick software purchase could thin our setter hours before any robot lifts a bar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect much of my setting pay to go early and most machine work to follow when robots can tend all three lathes. Maya’s wage and ten months saved help, but losing my higher wage would end our mortgage plan; I remember the last closure and would lie awake again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the planned summer trip, keep paid shifts while offered, and put new surplus wages into the reserve. If my hours are cut, I would apply for posted reachable machining or maintenance work only where the pay covers our bills, and ask the union to press for wage support before the last shift ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by that expected large wage loss. A reserve buys months, not another occupation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you abandon the CAM course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pause an unaccepted place because AGI could write those programs by 2028. If a paid course led to a posted maintenance job at adequate pay, I would assess it, but no such offer exists yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Maya work more shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She could ask the hospital, but the rota and children’s care must fit. I would not count extra nursing wages before they appear on her payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I will still be paying the mortgage and helping Sofia and Daniel through school. A maintenance ticket might buy some paid years if an employer needs people to repair robot cells, but I cannot assume it will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would review posted reachable maintenance vacancies and their wages this year. If the college offers a funded course with a real seat outside my paid shifts, Maya’s rota covers the children and a posted job pays our bills, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that job and keep my lathe shifts until an offer comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but five years gives me time to see whether the maintenance posts exist. I do not want to buy a certificate that ends up in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at postings first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last plant promised retraining after its big customer left, and the nearby jobs paid far less. I want a wage and travel time on paper before taking a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work on robot cells?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with an isolated machine and a qualified fitter teaching the first repair. I would learn those controls if the funded course actually provides that safe practical place.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: persona

In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare actual hours with posted local jobs; if shifts shrink, I would apply only for safe reachable work at a wage our household can live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about the distant change while our current wages stay secure. I want the kids to see us make choices from actual work, not a rumour about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would get the pension figures and mortgage balance first. If those numbers cannot cover our bills, I will keep looking for paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to secure?

transcript.speaker: persona

closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona

closing.speaker: persona

name: Beth Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and run a die-cutting press for printed food labels. My vocational certificate covered blade settings and safe stops; I like finding a perfect colour match, but clearing a torn roll from the guarded feed takes patience. I'm experienced and about average on the line, so I still ask the setter to verify tricky dies.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works regular school-kitchen hours. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about nine months of expenses saved. The press role pays above the ordinary operator rate and there are plenty of similar printers nearby. I use AI every day to sort defect logs, then check the pattern against actual sheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the label crew the AI log saves me a few minutes finding repeat colour faults, but a printed label still needs the right shade and a clean cut. If the big claims fade, that is fine. Our hands still check the first sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The die-cutting role pays above the usual operator rate, we have about nine months of expenses saved, and my partner has regular hours at a school kitchen. We have two school-age children and a mortgage, but our current wages cover them. There are plenty of similar plants nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the label die and checking the first printed sheet against the customer sample. I use AI daily to sort defect notes and will keep verifying each suggested pattern against the actual sheets. I'll bring the uneven-colour example to our union shift meeting about paid inspection time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job and our finances. I like a tool that saves counting, but I still want a person to sign the sample.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which defect did the log reveal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Monday the log showed colour drift on the late run, and the first sheet had a pale corner. We stopped to clean the ink roller before printing the full batch. A label with a pale corner is a real defect, even when the dashboard is green.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the household feel secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our nine-month cushion came from years of two wages and careful spending. The mortgage is still there, and we use the school-kitchen rota to plan child pickup. Right now neither job looks like it is disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The forming shift looks secure if AI stays modest. My wage is good, our eight-month reserve gives space, and there are other plants nearby. I would still watch Dan’s paid invoices rather than treat his next customer as money in the bank.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on a normal factory day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a robot welding cell for farm-trailer frames. The arm lays the long seams; I clamp steel in a jig, check the bead, and mend awkward corners by hand. I have a vocational certificate and know the settings well enough to spot a bad clamp before the robot runs. I enjoy the first clean seam on a new trailer model.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else matters around that shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Hana and I have two children in school and a mortgage. My welding-cell pay is good, and we have about nine months of expenses saved; Hana works, but I budget the house on my known wage rather than guessing what she might earn next month. I use AI every day for manuals and setup notes, then test every suggestion safely. On weekends I print replacement plastic clips for old motorbikes and sell a few online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the welders AI remains a decent manual search, not a magic torch. The jig still has to hold the frame square before the robot starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cell needs an operator and my wage looks sound if AI stays modest. Nine months saved lets us absorb a quiet spell, and there are other factories nearby. I would still like a better tool for finding a faulty seam, but I do not need it to pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.text: I would keep setting the welding cell, checking the seams and selling printed motorbike clips on weekends. If spring orders cover the printer’s parts and postage, I would buy a second printer from those profits to fill more paid orders.

transcript.text: I feel calm about work and the mortgage. A slower technology story would be a little dull, but a sound weld is enough excitement on some mornings.

transcript.text: Would the new printer have paying work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would order it only after I have enough spring clip orders to keep the first printer busy for several weekends. A spare machine on a shelf earns nothing. I can show Hana the actual invoices before buying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the AI assistant make you faster on the cell already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me find a manual page, but I still check the fixture and the weld test myself. I cannot send a trailer frame out because a chat box called it sound. The cell log has measured results for that reason.

transcript.text: How does the repair shop affect the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona

She and her bakery-worker partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage on low pay with three weeks saved.
Her **centre outlook** favors real numbers, while daily AI use helps her sort defect photos without replacing physical tests.
Fast robots make her **alarmed** about crew cuts; few local plants make offered paid training and posted jobs important.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable glass-forming robots around 2031 and cut household wages before savings grow.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing plan**, offered funded paid practical training and posted safe local work at sufficient base pay would help.

name: Carlos Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and lead a brick-press line. My two-year technical diploma covered mould dimensions and safe stops; other operators call me when a hollow block comes out lopsided. I like a strong clean first brick, but digging wet clay out of a jammed mould at shift end is miserable.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner takes sewing alterations at home. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about three weeks of expenses saved. The lead wage here is low for my skill and there are few similar plants nearby. I never use AI tools; I measure a bad brick and ask the owner about pay directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the brick crew a computer can print a kiln list, but it cannot tell whether a pressed brick crumbles in your hand. We still need a first-block test. I'd say the pay should match the people who keep the moulds square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the brick press with a two-year technical diploma, and other operators ask me to reset stubborn moulds. The lead rate here is below what this skill earns elsewhere, yet there are few brick works nearby. My partner takes sewing repairs at home; with two school-age children, a mortgage and three weeks saved, each bill matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the press and breaking a sample brick after each mould change. I'll ask the owner for a written lead-rate review at month's end. I never use AI tools; I learn more from the grit in a failed block than an office chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the money we already need, not the small AI change. I want the press paid fairly while it still runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the first brick show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A batch looked fine until the corner of the first cooled brick broke under a light tap. I found the mould edge had shifted and stopped the line before a pallet was stacked. A cracked brick hidden in a wall will not become strong later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does alteration work affect cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's alteration work is paid piece by piece, and some weeks no one brings a coat in. I budget from my low factory wage and put the mortgage first. We have less than a month saved, so I ask before buying school shoes.

transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the owner for the proposed base shifts and compare them with my last three wage slips. I'll keep the press checks. If the factory requires training on a new guarded mould changer and offers a paid trainer-led place on a stopped machine, I'll attend; I won't buy an AI course on my own time.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. transcript.text: I'll ask the owner now for written notice and any paid quality roles. We'll postpone replacing the kitchen floor to keep cash for the mortgage. If a funded paid-time course in brick testing offers a guarded practical place, I'll enrol; if my press hours end, I'll apply for posted safe local production jobs only if regular pay and school hours cover our bills, and after qualifying I'll apply for posted local testing jobs under the same terms.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course should make me test a brick's strength, spot a shifted corner and stop the press safely. A trainer must watch me reject a bad batch on a guarded line. I could not pay tuition from three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fallback job would you consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The production fallback has to be posted nearby with a base rate and safe work. I would compare its shift with school pickup and my partner's sewing customers. An overtime promise is not enough to replace the lead wage.

name: Jade Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary factory day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead four operators on plastic injection moulding machines that make appliance handles. A machine closes a mould, injects hot plastic, cools it and opens again; I set the heat and pressure and check each batch for warping. My two-year technical diploma helped, but the crew calls me when a handle twists because I have worked the faults for twelve years. I like getting a clean batch on time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do the shifts fit your home life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Joel does garden maintenance, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My senior operator wage is low for what I do; we have less than one month of expenses saved, and there are few similar plants nearby. Joel gets more paid work in spring than winter. I use AI occasionally to check an unfamiliar fault code, but I will not change a heater setting until I read the machine manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the headlines were louder than the change, and a mould still needs a person who sees a warped handle. A phone answer is no substitute for the manual at a hot machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to keep this skilled job if AI stays small, but our pay is already tight. Joel’s gardening slows in winter, and less than a month saved barely covers a furnace repair at home. The mortgage is the thing I think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the moulding machines and teach the new operator how to spot warping before a box is filled. From each paid spring garden job after fuel and tools, Joel and I would transfer a fixed amount into a winter cash account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our existing bills, though the factory work itself feels familiar. I can hear the next mortgage payment before I hear an AI warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a bad batch cost last month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A heater drifted and curled the handles on three racks. We stopped the press, reset the temperature and saved the rest of the order. My diploma gave me the theory; my crew and I did the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a small AI tool help with that fault?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe as a second opinion on a code, after I check the manual. I have seen an app name a sensor our press does not have. I would never let a vague answer overrule a warped handle in my hand.

name: Rafael Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on an ordinary factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the shift on circular knitting machines that make workwear fabric. Yarn feeds through a ring of needles, and I set tension, change feeders and check the cloth for repeating holes. I have a two-year technical diploma and I am the person called when a machine starts dropping stitches at full speed. Solving that before a roll is ruined is the best part of my day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the job sit alongside home life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Nora works part time at a grocer, and we have two children at school and a mortgage. I am one of the strongest setters at this plant, yet the wage is low for a senior operator and we have less than a month put aside. Only a few similar mills are nearby. I use AI every day to search fault logs and compare settings, then inspect the fabric myself. My father taught me that a good trade should support a family, so I notice when it does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the mill crew that AI is a useful search box, but it has not learned to feel a loose stitch on a running roll. I would keep using it for fault logs without treating it like a setter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead work to continue, but our mortgage is too close to the end of each pay packet. Nora’s shop hours can change, and we have less than a month saved. A quiet AI year would still make me watch the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the knitting machines and write down which fault-log checks prevented scrap. I would use those figures to apply for a posted shift supervisor role if its wage covers the mortgage and its hours fit school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household money, not the machine. A loose stitch is easier to fix than a missing grocery shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the supervisor job change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might pay enough to get ahead of the mortgage for once. I would still walk the floor, but I would be responsible for two shifts rather than one. I need the posted wage before I say yes to more responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the AI tool already catch dropped stitches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It finds a page in the manual faster than I can. The camera catches a pattern, then I check the yarn feeder and the cloth. A screen cannot tell me which operator has been fighting the same needle all morning.

opening.text: I lead a corrugated-box die-cutting line at a packaging factory. opening.text: How does that work fit around home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nadia works reception at a dental practice, and our two children are still at school. name: Bianca Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, still a junior operator on a soap-bottling line. I finished secondary school and moved over from packing only eight months ago. I load caps, watch the fill marks and call the setter when bottles jam; I like getting a whole batch through without leaks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and where does AI fit in?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband repairs bicycles on short shop hours, and our grown children live on their own. We rent, have less than one month of expenses saved and my operator pay is low. There are few bottling plants within a sensible journey. I use AI every day to explain machine words and plan errands, but I check instructions with the setter. I'd like to stop at 67, if a real household income calculation says we can pay our way.

opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, separate from employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I tend a coil-winding machine that winds copper wire for small electric motors. I thread the spool, watch the tension and count damaged windings before the coils go to assembly. I joined after a warehouse job and am still the junior operator at 58, learning how different wire gauges behave. I finished secondary school and earn an ordinary machine-operator wage.

opening.text: My partner Mariam works at a community kitchen, and our grown sons live on their own. We rent and have about three months of expenses saved; there are some similar plants near us. I use AI every day to explain diagrams and put my shift notes in order, then check any winding setting with the printed sheet and a trainer. I like trying a new tool early, but I keep a hand away from a moving spindle until somebody shows me a safe stop. We talk about retirement, though no amount is settled.

name: Hana Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is your usual shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, 58, and I run a small coffee-roasting drum at a food factory. I finished secondary school and moved from bag packing onto the roaster eight months ago, so I still ask the lead to check my first temperature curve. I like hearing the beans crack at the right moment, but I have scorched a batch by opening the door too late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do the job and family money fit, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Farid works regular hospital porter shifts, and our children are grown and living elsewhere. I earn about the normal rate for a roaster operator, we have four months of expenses saved and some other food plants nearby. I use AI every day to explain roast-log patterns, then compare them with the colour and smell of a sample. We talk about retirement, but we have not matched any estimate to our actual bills yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI can tidy roast logs, but the beans still have to be cooled and checked before they go into bags. A little help with order sheets would leave our shift much the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two regular wages cover rent and food, and four months saved gives us breathing room. The mild AI picture would not threaten my hours, though I am still learning how this drum behaves after a dark roast. I can ask a person on the line when a graph looks odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the roaster and showing the first cooling tray to the lead. I already use AI each day to read logs, so I would carry on checking its ideas against the beans; I would add a small new amount from each full paid month to our reserve after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The machine would still need my hands, and Farid's hospital wage is steady at the moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a log fail to tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the curve looked fine, but the first tray smelled burnt because I had left the drum door closed too long. I held the batch while the lead checked it. A clean roast graph cannot take the burnt taste out of a coffee bean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you add to the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only from new pay after rent, food and power. The four months already saved would stay for a gap in wages; moving them to another account would not build a new cushion.

name: Erik Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What does your factory work involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a router that cuts cabinet panels from boards. I load the board, check the jig and measure the first slot before the panels go to assembly. I came in after delivery work and am a junior operator at 58, still learning how the wood behaves under a fresh bit. I finished secondary school and my wage is about ordinary for this job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and how do you use new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Clara works a pharmacy counter, and our grown children live nearby but support their own homes. We have a mortgage and just under four months of expenses saved. A few other wood-products plants are within a reasonable trip, if they have actual openings. I ask an AI tool almost every day to explain a router code or sketch a checklist, but I check every dimension against the drawing and ask the setter before changing a bit. I like trying things early, as long as the guard stays on and someone knows how to stop the machine. We would like to ease out of shifts later, but have not priced that yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the cabinet crew that faster office plans do not make a board square. We still have to measure the first routed slot and keep the bit guarded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two pay packets cover the mortgage and nearly four months saved is a useful cushion. I am new to routing and need work time to get good at it. This quiet picture gives me that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm enough. I can learn the machine in stages without my hours changing suddenly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is your first check on a panel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I put the gauge into the first slot before the next board is fed. A cabinet panel can look straight and still leave a hinge sitting crooked. The setter taught me to measure before admiring the finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run an AI-generated router programme?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not directly. I ask the tool what a code means, then compare the programme with the approved drawing and the setter’s instructions. A clever sentence does not measure a slot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What happens on your normal factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Dana, 58, and I feed dough into a biscuit divider on nights. I finished secondary school and came to this machine from packing less than a year ago, so the lead still checks my first tray after a size change. I like seeing each biscuit land in the same place; a sticky roller can turn a whole batch into crumbs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are your pay, home and use of new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leon works daytime maintenance in a hospital, and our grown children live elsewhere. The night premium gives me higher pay than most operators, we have about ten months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other food plants nearby. I use AI occasionally to make sense of an oven notice, after a colleague checks it; I would not set the divider from a chat answer. Retirement is approaching as a decision, but we have not compared the actual income with our rent and living costs.

transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The night rate and Leon's hospital pay cover our rent, and ten months saved gives us a buffer if a line stops. This small office change would not shorten my hours. I am still learning the divider, which is quite enough novelty for some shifts.

transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.text: Only if the employer offered paid safe instruction and I still needed the job. The practical inspection course is more useful to me than experimenting with a screen I have never used.

say: I would separate **2036 order AGI** from physical kiln robots around 2039.
A decade allows **income checks** while firing work still pays.
think: At **71**, I may have stopped if written income covers costs.
Our **current wages** and three months saved cover near-term bills.
do: **Keep** safe paid kiln shifts and request written retirement figures.
**Take** accepted inspection training only with funded paid guarded practice.
**Apply** after 2036 cuts if working to posted safe local jobs at viable net pay.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work while the present household bills are covered.
S4.quote: I want the income numbers before I give up the familiar kiln.
fieldNote: His **retirement enquiry** is not an exit promise; earlier stopping requires written income after housing and health costs.
Later **training and applications** remain conditional on paid safe places or real local job postings with viable net wages.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and household cost figures this year
Retire before 2039 only if reliable written income covers housing food and health costs
Take accepted inspection course only if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply after 2036 cuts if working to posted safe local work if net pay fits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 AGI picture worries me most because robots around 2031 could take away the kiln shifts before June and I can afford to stop. A funded paid inspection place with safe practice, written staffing dates and posted local jobs at enough net pay would help. I will not leave my current shift for a brochure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether the new loader can tell a hot cracked tile from a sound one. Someone still has to hold the bad pallet before it reaches a customer's floor.

headlineQuote: Someone still has to hold the bad pallet before it reaches a customer's floor.
portrait: **Carlos**, 58, is an experienced mid-level ceramic-tile kiln operator with a vocational certificate and average practical skill.
He and his **partner June** have grown daughters, typical operator pay, about three months saved and some other nearby plants.
He has **never used AI**, prefers a temperature log and tile sample, and will consider only proven paid safe instruction.
Expected **2031 physical robots** threaten kiln shifts; stopping earlier depends on written retirement income covering costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 kiln robots** could remove his paid physical shifts before retirement income or another adequate local wage is clear.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written staffing dates**, accepted funded practical inspection training on paid time and posted safe local jobs with adequate net pay.
